title: The work belongs to someone else
brief: A job needs an agent that another team, vendor or framework owns. You cannot inspect its prompts, tools or memory. Whether you call it as a function, as an MCP tool or as a peer depends on ownership, task shape and how much of its internals you control.

blocks.md:
**A2A** is an open protocol for communication between independent, often opaque agent systems. Its design goals include opaque execution, support for long-running and human-in-the-loop work, and several interaction modes: request and response, streaming and push notifications [[r1]]. Google created it in April 2025 and the Linux Foundation launched the A2A project on 2025-06-23, citing more than 100 supporting companies [[r9]]. Version 1.0.0 was released on 2026-03-12 and the patch 1.0.1 on 2026-05-28 [[r4]].

The official comparison draws the line by direction. **MCP is vertical**: it deepens one agent with tools and resources. **A2A is horizontal**: it connects agents across a boundary, such as another team, department or organization. Inside each agent you keep using MCP, and between agents you use A2A [[r3]].

blocks.title: MCP inside an agent, A2A between agents
blocks.alt: Agent A uses MCP to reach its own tools and uses A2A to talk to Agent B, which belongs to another team. Agent B uses MCP to reach its own tools.
blocks.src:
flowchart LR
  UA[User] --> A[Agent A]
  A -->|MCP| T1[Tools of A]
  A -->|A2A| B[Agent B]
  B -->|MCP| T2[Tools of B]
blocks.caption: Agent B stays opaque. Agent A sees skills and results, not B's tools, prompts or memory [[r3]].

blocks.title: Three ways to use another agent
blocks.intro: Wrap it as an in-process tool, put it behind MCP, or call it as an A2A peer.

options.name: Agent as an in-process tool
options.summary: Wrap the other agent as a function tool inside one process.
pros: No network hop and shared tracing
cons: Couples release cycles, language and runtime
No protocol-level task lifecycle. You build your own
options.bestWhen: Both agents live in one process and one team maintains them [[r13]].
options.avoidWhen: Separate release cycles, owners or languages.

options.name: Agent behind an MCP tool
options.summary: Expose the agent as an MCP tool so any MCP host can call it.
pros: Reuses MCP hosts, auth profile and gateways
Fits a stateless, well-defined request and result
cons: A tool call has no task lifecycle unless both sides support the Tasks extension [[r20]]
options.bestWhen: The agent behaves like a function with a fixed input and output.
options.avoidWhen: Work is multi-turn, long-running or produces artifacts that need tracking.

options.name: A2A peer
options.summary: Discover the agent through its card and exchange messages and tasks.
pros: Cards for discovery, a task lifecycle, input-required, artifacts
Streaming, push, versioning and signing are in the spec
cons: Network latency, retries, timeouts and version management
Platform support varies. Foundry incoming A2A is JSON-RPC, text only, with no streaming [[r17]]
options.bestWhen: You cross a service, team or organization boundary [[r12]].
options.avoidWhen: A shared process and team make a function call enough.

blocks.title: Pick the boundary
blocks.prompt: Flip who owns the other agent, the shape of the work and how much of its internals you control.

blocks.takeaway: Cross a boundary only when you must. Ownership and work shape decide between a function, a tool and a peer.

blocks.title: Failure modes and how to detect them

items.symptom: The calling agent times out on a 20-minute job
items.cause: A peer was treated like a function and called synchronously through a tool wrapper
items.fix: Use tasks: return a handle, then poll, stream or use push. Detect it with a timeout rate per remote skill

items.symptom: Every user request pays an extra network round trip to a helper agent that lives in the same repo
items.cause: A network boundary was introduced where none existed
items.fix: Collapse same-team agents into in-process tools and keep A2A for real boundaries

items.symptom: A wrapped MCP tool loses the result when the client disconnects
items.cause: No task lifecycle, so the work is tied to one connection
items.fix: Use the Tasks extension on both sides, or call the agent through A2A tasks

items.symptom: A trace shows a gap where the remote agent ran
items.cause: Opaque execution hides internals, and trace context was not propagated
items.fix: Propagate W3C trace context in HTTP headers and log `taskId` and correlation ids on both sides [[r8]]

items.symptom: An agent call returns inconsistent totals
items.cause: A deterministic lookup was given to an LLM agent
items.fix: Use a plain API when the work is deterministic

items.label: Linux Foundation launch
items.note: More than 100 supporting companies at launch [[r9]]

blocks.title: A2A does not replace MCP
blocks.md: If asked "A2A or MCP?", answer with the boundary. Tools and resources for one agent use MCP. Independent agents that own their own reasoning and state use A2A. A2A's own comparison notes that well-defined, stateless skills can also be surfaced through MCP-style descriptions, but that gives up the task lifecycle [[r3]].

quiz.q: What does **opaque execution** mean in A2A?
options: Agents encrypt every message end to end so that network monitoring tools, gateways and auditors cannot read any traffic between them at all
Agents collaborate through declared capabilities and exchanged messages without sharing internal reasoning, memory or tool implementations
Agent Cards must not describe skills
Every task is executed on the caller's infrastructure
quiz.explain: Opacity is about internals: callers see skills, messages and artifacts, not prompts, plans or tools. It does not mean hiding traffic from monitoring, and cards still describe skills. The remote agent runs on its own infrastructure.

quiz.q: Select every situation where an A2A peer is a better boundary than an in-process agent-as-tool.
options: The other agent has its own release cycle and a different owning team
A partner organization's agent was built in another framework and language
Two agents share a process and are maintained by one team
The remote work takes minutes, may ask the caller questions and returns files
The call is a deterministic lookup with a fixed schema
quiz.explain: Separate owners, cross-organization interoperability and a long-running, interactive, artifact-producing job all justify A2A. A shared process and team favors agent-as-tool, and a deterministic lookup is best served by a plain API.

quiz.q: Another team's agent runs 15-minute analyses, may ask clarifying questions and returns reports. You can reach it only over HTTPS. Which boundary fits best?
options: A2A peer with tasks, `input-required` handling and artifacts
An in-process function wrapper that blocks until the report is ready
An MCP tool call that returns when the report is finished, with no task support
A plain API call to its web UI
quiz.explain: The dials say another team, long-running, interactive and opaque, which is the A2A sweet spot. A blocking wrapper or a no-task MCP call ties the result to one connection and cannot ask questions. A web UI is not a contract.

quiz.q: Match each need to the boundary that fits best.

pairs.l: Give one agent a database query capability
Let a partner's agent take a task and return artifacts
Call a helper agent in the same process and team
Fetch a price with a fixed schema

quiz.explain: MCP deepens one agent with tools and data. A2A connects independent agents with tasks and artifacts. Agent-as-tool is the simplest in one process. A deterministic call needs no agent at all.

takeaways: MCP is vertical and gives one agent tools. A2A is horizontal and connects independent, opaque agents.
Use an in-process tool when one team owns both agents. Use A2A when you cross a service, team or organization boundary.
A tool call has no task lifecycle unless the Tasks extension is supported. A2A has tasks, contexts and artifacts built in.
A2A v1.0.0 was released on 2026-03-12 and v1.0.1 on 2026-05-28.
